title: Genomic signatures associated with small-scale farming landscapes in wild bee populations: potential adaptive response under high gene flow
authors: Paulo O, Henriques A, Sousa P, Silva S, Galhofa D, Carvalheiro L, Wood T, Rollin O.
abstract:
Abstract

Intensified agricultural landscapes can influence both genetic diversity and signatures of selection in wild bees, yet the genomic consequences of retaining small-scale farming (SSF) landscapes remain poorly understood. We used RAD sequencing to investigate population structure, genetic diversity, signatures of selection, and genotype-environment associations in three widespread wild bee species sampled across contrasting SSF and low-agricultural (LoA) landscapes in Portugal: Andrena flavipes Panzer, 1799, Bombus terrestris (Linnaeus, 1758), and Lasioglossum malachurum (Kirby, 1802). Across species, genetic diversity was high and comparable between SSF and LoA landscapes, genetic differentiation was low, population structure was weak, and isolation by distance was not detected, suggesting high connectivity among sampling locations. Complementary selection detection approaches identified conservative sets of candidate SNPs associated with land-use contrasts and composite gradients of landscape configuration. Functional annotation of overlapping candidate SNPs identified genes involved in signaling, cellular communication, ion transport, metabolism, transcriptional regulation, and sensory or stress-related processes. Our results suggest that SSF landscapes may maintain genetic diversity while also being associated with genomic signatures that provide a basis for future studies of wild bee adaptation.

title: Genotype imputation improves GWAS resolution and facilitates candidate gene identification in pearl millet
authors: Kambara K, Gupta SK, Tsugama D.
abstract:
Pearl millet ( Cenchrus americanus ; syn. Pennisetum glaucum (L.) R. Br.) is an important cereal crop mainly grown in semi-arid areas. However, in pearl millet, genes underlying many agronomic traits remain unknown. Our previous genome-wide association study (GWAS) was based primarily on genotype data derived from restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (RAD-seq), which contained a high proportion of missing genotypes and may have limited mapping resolution. To address this limitation, we used whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-derived genotype data from 21 elite lines as a reference panel to impute missing genotypes in the RAD-seq-derived dataset. Genotype imputation reduced the proportion of missing genotypes from 82.42% to 0% and increased the mean density of non-missing genotypes from 569.61 to 1,158.09 genotypes/Mb. Leave-one-out validation yielded a mean genotype concordance of 89.9 ± 4.6%. GWAS using the imputed dataset showed more localized association signals for several traits. Homologs of rice SHORT INTERNODES1 , Arabidopsis FLOWERING LOCUS Y , and rice EPIDERMAL PATTERNING FACTOR 2 were identified as candidates for genes regulating culm height, days to panicle emergence, and awn growth, respectively. These results demonstrate that reference-panel-based genotype imputation can increase the utility of reduced-representation genotype datasets and facilitate candidate gene identification in pearl millet.

Key message Imputation of missing genotypes in RAD-seq-derived genotype data using a WGS-derived reference panel improved GWAS resolution and facilitated candidate gene identification for agronomic traits in pearl millet.

title: Host-tree association and evolutionary history shape components of genomic diversity across a saproxylic beetle assemblage
authors: Krovi R, Amer N, Wierzbicka A, Szmatoła T, Oczkowicz M, Plewa R, Jaworski T, Kadej M, Smolis A, Kajtoch Ł.
abstract:
Abstract

Intraspecific genetic diversity is a crucial yet incompletely mapped component of biodiversity, and comparative studies frequently treat heterozygosity and nucleotide diversity as interchangeable despite their differing genomic denominators and demographic timescales. Using a standardized de novo ddRAD-seq workflow, we generated genome-wide data for 759 individuals representing 149 populations, 26 saproxylic beetle species and 14 families across eight forest complexes, and tested whether species occurrence, host-tree association and phylogenetic history predict distinct components of genomic diversity. Population-level linear mixed models ranked the intercept-only null model highest for all-position nucleotide diversity (π), variant-site observed and expected heterozygosity (H o and H e ) and the inbreeding coefficient (F IS ), indicating that species identity and site structure govern most variance. Species-level Phylogenetic Generalized Least-Squares models, however, resolved a clear division among metrics: H e was significantly elevated in deciduous-associated species relative to conifer specialists, whereas π carried a consistent phylogenetic signal that persisted after excluding the influential lineage Rhysodes sulcatus . Occurrence tier predicted no metric after correction, and forest-management effects were minor and confounded with forest-complex identity. Ecological and evolutionary predictors thus shape distinct components of genomic diversity: H e aligns with contemporary ecological association, while π reflects shared evolutionary history.

title: Population genetic structure of three species of declining North American swallows: Implications for conservation and management
authors: Lekamlage T, Kardynal K, Hobson K, Mitchell G, Burg T.
abstract: North American aerial insectivorous birds have suffered steep population declines over the last half-century. Limited information on the population genetic structure of many aerial insectivores restricts our ability to understand factors affecting population-specific trends and infer population connectivity. To address this gap, we examined the population genetic structure of barn (Hirundo rustica erythrogaster), bank (Riparia riparia riparia), and tree (Tachycineta bicolor) swallows across their breeding ranges in North America. We used restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (RADseq) and higher-resolution low-coverage whole genome sequencing (lcWGS) to study species-specific population genetic structure. Additionally, we used species distribution models (SDM) to determine the potential for Pleistocene glacial refugia as drivers of genetic variation. Multivariate analyses identified population clusters corresponding to western, central, and eastern North America for barn and bank swallows, and shallower structure for tree swallows. Species-specific SDMs provided evidence that suitable habitat for both barn and bank swallows existed in multiple refugia during the Pleistocene, and likely either a single southern refugium or higher gene flow after recolonization for tree swallows, supporting the genetic patterns in our data. Our results suggest historical events, physical barriers and migratory pathways continue to shape and maintain population genetic structure among swallow populations. Our findings can be used to guide future sampling of populations to further differentiate genetic structure and serve as a ‘genoscape’ for studies assessing migratory connectivity of individuals sampled during the non-breeding season.

title: Genomic dissection of environmental responsiveness and cross-environment productivity in fenugreek
authors: Aljabri M, Abd El-Wahab MMH, Dobeie AM, El-Soda M.
abstract: Dissecting the genetic basis of genotype × environment interaction (G × E) is important for breeding crops with stable or responsive performance across production environments. Using previously published seed-yield data from 107 Egyptian fenugreek accessions evaluated under two contrasting field environments, we investigated whether yield potential and environmental responsiveness share a common genetic basis. Seed yield per plant was measured in Giza (SYP_G; reference environment) and Wadi El-Natrun (SYP_W; contrasting environment). Nine derived indices were calculated to characterize environmental responsiveness, productivity, and stability: relative performance index (RPI), yield plasticity index (YPI), stress tolerance index (STI), log response ratio (LRR), mean productivity (MP), harmonic mean (HM), tolerance index (TOL), stress susceptibility index (SSI), and AMMI stability value (ASV). The near-zero correlation between SYP_G and SYP_W (r = 0.107) indicated substantial genotype reranking across environments, while several response indices were closely related to SYP_W and therefore predominantly reflected environment-dependent yield expression. Phenotypic analyses also identified contrasting performance strategies, ranging from highly responsive accessions, such as G15 (RPI = 3.629), to highly stable accessions, such as G41 (YPI = 0.001). These phenotypes were integrated with 38,142 SNPs using univariate association-mapping approaches. In addition, SYP_G and SYP_W were subjected to multivariate association-mapping. Association mapping identified one genome-wide-significant SNP for STI and several suggestive loci showed concordant associations across mapping methods. Within the current panel, marker coverage, and significance thresholds, most adaptation-index associations did not overlap previously reported yield loci; however, dDocent_Contig_39939_66, previously associated with seed yield in this panel, also showed cross-method suggestive associations with RPI and TOL. Comparative genomic analysis of three legume reference genomes supported two gene-linked candidate loci associated with STI: a cation/H⁺ antiporter and an importin subunit beta-1. The same analysis classified two of the strongest statistical signals, including the sole genome-wide-significant locus, as repetitive or transposable-element sequences rather than single-copy genes. These findings demonstrate that statistical association strength does not necessarily establish a coding-gene basis for loci identified using reference-free ddRAD markers. Within the current population size and marker coverage, environmental responsiveness and productivity appeared partially distinct but biologically connected components of environment-dependent yield performance. The results provide a genomic and phenotypic framework for prioritizing fenugreek germplasm for further evaluation while emphasizing the need for independent-population, multi-season, and functional validation of the identified candidate loci.

title: Genome-wide selection signatures in Turkish Awassi sheep: uncovering the genetic basis of production traits and adaptation
authors: Meydan H, Demir E, Bilginer Ü, Doğru H, Kaya S, Argun Karsli B, Aktaş Y, Atmaca V, Perini F, Karsli T.
abstract: The Awassi sheep is one of the leading fat-tailed breeds of the Fertile Crescent, known for its high milk yield and resilience in arid and semi-arid environments. Despite its socio-economic importance, a high-resolution genomic characterization of selection signatures in Turkish Awassi populations remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the genomic diversity, demographic history, and selection signatures of Turkish Awassi sheep using double-digest restriction-site-associated DNA sequencing (ddRADseq). Genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) discovery was performed on 40 unrelated Awassi sheep. Genetic diversity parameters, historical effective population size ( Ne ), and linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay were assessed. Selection signatures were identified using both runs of homozygosity (ROH) islands and Tajima's D analyses, followed by functional annotation of candidate genes. A total of 397 315 high-quality SNPs were identified. The average minor allele frequency (MAF) was 0.333, and the ROH-based inbreeding coefficient ( FROH ) was low (0.025), indicating high genetic integrity. The historical Ne showed a consistent decline, reaching 147 in the most recent generations. Selection signature analysis identified 21 and 48 protein-coding genes by means of ROH and Tajima's D , respectively. The key candidate genes were associated with milk yield and lactation (AKR1C3, AKR1D1, OXT, AVP, ZNF131), meat production and growth (PBX1, KBTBD8, HOXA cluster, ADGB), fat-tail formation (HOXA cluster, HMGCS1, STARD4), and environmental adaptation (ABCB1, TSLP, IL6). Our findings reveal that the Turkish Awassi genome is a rich genetic reservoir shaped by combined natural and artificial selection. The selection signatures identified in this study provide fundamental genomic targets for future breeding strategies to enhance productivity without compromising environmental resilience. These findings support the use of Turkish Awassi as a genetic resource for breeding programs in arid and semi-arid production systems.

title: Breeding Behaviors and Kinship in the Endangered Hawaiian Stilt (Ae'o; Himantopus mexicanus knudseni)
authors: Price MR, Harmon KC, Toonen RJ, Freel EB, Emms MA, Dudoit ', Loockerman C, Dibben-Young A.
abstract: Understanding the genetic underpinnings of cooperative and noncooperative breeding behaviors is critical for species of conservation concern. We investigated the genetic relatedness of Hawaiian Stilts (Ae'o; Himantopus mexicanus knudseni), a threatened subspecies restricted to the Hawaiian Islands, in relation to nesting behavior, given recent behavioral observations of cooperative breeding, potential conspecific brood parasitism, and potential pairing of closely related individuals for nesting. Using RAD sequencing of blood and feather samples, we generated ~6800 SNPs for parentage and relatedness analysis. Observational data documented behaviors including cooperative incubation, helpers-at-the-nest, and potential conspecific brood parasitism, which are rarely reported in Charadriiformes. Parentage, genomic relatedness, and Bayesian phylogenetic analyses revealed instances of conspecific brood parasitism and potential extra-pair paternity. We also find evidence of inbreeding, with an overall F IS of 0.23 and close genetic similarity between some mates. Ecological constraints and limited dispersal opportunities may promote cooperative breeding, conspecific brood parasitism, and inbreeding in Hawaiian Stilts. These results underscore the importance of maintaining and restoring nesting habitat to reduce pressures that may otherwise intensify inbreeding in this recovering population but also highlight the behavioral flexibility and adaptive capacity in this species.

title: Ancestral introgression and dual mitochondrial capture shaped mito-nuclear discordance in sky-island skinks (Scincidae: Sphenomorphus)
authors: Lin TH, Wang YT, Liao PC, Nguyen HN, Tseng HY, Lin SM.
journal: Evolution; international journal of organic evolution
abstract: Mito-nuclear discordance can obscure the interpretation of evolutionary history, particularly in fragmented systems where multiple processes can generate similar phylogenetic patterns. We investigated pronounced discordance between mitochondrial and nuclear genomes in two parapatric montane skinks, Sphenomorphus taiwanensis and S. luelaiorum, from Taiwan's sky islands. Using mitochondrial sequences and genome-wide ddRAD-seq SNPs, we evaluated incomplete lineage sorting, introgression, and ghost introgression as alternative explanations, while assessing sex-biased dispersal, selection, and demographic history. Model-based analyses supported historical introgression between extant lineages but provided little evidence for ghost introgression. An expanded coalescent analysis favored bidirectional over unidirectional introgression. Genomic indices showed no consistent sex-biased dispersal, whereas mitochondrial selection signals were restricted to particular lineages. Coalescent estimates and forward simulations indicated that small effective population sizes could increase the probability of mitochondrial capture. We interpret the discordance as the outcome of ancestral bidirectional introgression followed by genetic drift in isolated montane populations, with selection potentially facilitating fixation under high-altitude conditions. These findings illustrate how gene flow and demographic processes in fragmented landscapes can generate persistent mito-nuclear discordance, underscoring the importance of integrating genomic and ecological evidence when interpreting mitochondrial phylogenies.

title: Species with U-shaped geographic ranges as an opportunity to study early stages of divergence: The case of Ipomoea microsepala
authors: Piña-de la Rosa IA, Cacho NI.
abstract:
Premise The study of the early stages of divergence between populations is crucial to understanding how species and biodiversity originate. Geographic distributions that capture some aspects of the process of divergence, such as those that are markedly U-shaped, could offer a window to identify systems undergoing incipient speciation, which have traditionally been difficult to identify.

Methods We selected Ipomoea microsepala, a species of morning-glory with a markedly U-shaped distribution, as a candidate to evaluate potential incipient evolutionary divergence. We used a combination of principal component, phylogenetic, population, and correlation analyses (Mantel tests) of data derived from leaf morphometrics, climatic information, and genome-wide DNA variation (RADseq) that span the whole species range to assess potential divergence in genomic, climatic, and morphological dimensions.

Results We showed that Ipomoea microsepala achieved its current geographic distribution through historical range expansion by successively colonizing adjacent areas in a fashion that is consistent with a stepping-stone model and isolation by distance. Phylogenetic and population genetic models supported three present leading fronts through which I. microsepala could continue to expand its range and diverge. Plants in these fronts are already genetically distinct, do not exhibit introgression, and use marginally different climate spaces, but lack differences in leaf morphology.

Conclusions A geographic perspective continues to be useful to identify and shed light on the process of divergence. Further ecological experimentation with a genomic perspective is necessary to assess the degree to which the differentiation we documented is congruent with early stages of speciation.

title: Ecological and Genomic Evidence of Cryptic Speciation in the Potato Psyllid (Bactericera cockerelli)
authors: Kenney JR, Scarparo G, Molfini M, Tran M, Tran S, Murguia S, Gebiola M, Sarkar P, Purcell J, Mauck KE.
abstract: The potato psyllid (Bactericera cockerelli) is a crop pest that serves as a vector for the bacterial pathogen Candidatus Liberibacter solanacearum (CLso), which causes disease in solanaceous and apiaceous crops. This psyllid species carries substantial haplotypic diversity based on mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase 1 (mtCOI) sequences, associated with strong geographic and temporal separation. Using mtCOI sequencing and genomic ddRADseq analysis of 111,587 SNPs across 590 individuals collected from native Solanaceae and cultivated crops at 50 geographically paired sites in California, we show that the previously described haplotype diversity in B. cockerelli may represent at least three genetically distinct cryptic species. These three lineages exhibited extremely high genomic F ST values across all 13 chromosomes and are strongly partitioned by the host plant. The Northwestern lineage is strictly associated with the native perennial Solanum umbelliferum, while the Western lineage is associated with solanaceous crops, and the Southwestern lineage moves between native and cultivated hosts in desert regions. Hybridization is also rare, suggesting reproductive isolation. SNP and divergence analyses for the obligate bacterial symbiont support conclusions of the host nuclear and mtCOI sequence analyses. We also detected five CLso variants in psyllid samples. The Northwestern lineage housed G, Sumb2, F and B variants, while the Western lineage housed only B and A variants. The largest diversity of CLso variants occurred in coastal regions where psyllid lineages overlap. Exploring the ecology and CLso associations of this potential cryptic species complex provides a foundation for improving biosecurity and management of potato psyllids and CLso pathogens.

title: Genome-wide population genomic analyses reveal extensive admixture and limited geographic structure in Australian Fasciola hepatica
authors: Zheng M, Sukee T, Taki AC, Hodgkinson JE, Paterson S, Spithill TW, Gasser RB, Young ND.
abstract: Fasciola hepatica is a globally important trematode parasite of livestock and humans, but its population structure in Australia remains unknown. In this study, double-digest restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (ddRADseq) was used to investigate population genomic structure and genetic diversity in 217 adult F. hepatica collected from cattle and sheep across New South Wales (NSW), Victoria (VIC) and Tasmania (TAS). After quality filtering and linkage disequilibrium pruning, 9,205 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were retained for analyses. Principal component analysis (PCA), fastSTRUCTURE and identity-by-state (IBS) analyses consistently revealed weak geographic structuring and extensive admixture among populations from southeast Australia. Although differentiated clusters were detected in Sunny Corner (NSW), with three Echuca (VIC) individuals also showing separation from the main cluster and a subset of Powranna (TAS) and Numbugga (NSW) individuals showing partial differentiation, most individuals exhibited substantial genetic overlap across populations. This genome-wide analysis provides an important genomic framework for future surveillance and improved understanding of the population biology and epidemiology of fascioliasis in Australia.

title: Genetic Diversity and Structure Analysis of Wild Oysters (Crassostrea virginica) Within and Between River Systems Reveals Spatial Genetic Structure and Salinity-Adaptive Variation Across the Canadian Maritimes
authors: Hall S, Méthé D, Steeves R, LaFlamme M, Dinn C, Sonier R, Clements JC.
abstract: In the Canadian Maritimes, the eastern oyster (Crassostrea virginica) industry has been shaped by population-scale events, including ~90% reductions of natural beds from Malpeque disease. For many years, Maritime oyster populations were considered genetically homogenous due to large-scale transplants to rehabilitate depleted beds; however, recent studies suggest that ancestral populations survived. We characterized genetic diversity and geographical genetic structure (using ddRAD-seq) of wild oysters from 24 locations (n = 1409) across New Brunswick (NB), Prince Edward Island (PEI), and Nova Scotia (NS), including multiple locations along estuarine gradients within the same river systems. While genetic differentiation was low between Maritime locations (F st = 0.012), ADMIXTURE analysis demonstrated spatial structure with cross-validation (CV) error optimized at K = 4 ancestral populations. Oysters from the Bras d'Or Lakes in NS, and Miramichi and Richibucto in NB were characterized by distinct dominant ancestries, whereas populations from Bouctouche and Caraquet in NB, the Foxley, Grand, and Brudenell Rivers on PEI, and Pictou in NS shared a common dominant ancestry. Populations from coastal Cape Breton (Aspy River and Arichat) in NS exhibited mixed ancestry, primarily consisting of Bras d'Or Lake and 'Gulf' lineages. Within estuaries, genetic differentiation between upriver and downriver sites was minimal (F st = 0.002-0.003), suggesting ongoing gene flow along estuarine gradients; however, each estuary contained a subset of SNP loci putatively under selection, indicating potential local adaptation despite high connectivity. Functional annotation of candidate loci identified genes associated with membrane transport, cellular stress response, protein turnover, and metabolic pathways, suggesting that environmental gradients may contribute to adaptive divergence. Ultimately, this reveals a complex genetic landscape and demonstrates that oyster beds in the Maritime provinces have retained genetic structure from both historical transfer activity in the region and local adaptation. The results provide important insights for the conservation, management, and restoration of eastern oyster populations throughout Atlantic Canada.

title: Isolation to extinction: landscape fragmentation and connectivity in sloth bears of the Indian Terai
authors: Rana D, Samjith JC, Ramakrishnan U.
abstract: Habitat fragmentation is a major global threat to biodiversity, leading to small and isolated populations. Fragmented landscapes can reduce connectivity, erode genetic diversity, and increase inbreeding risk, potentially contributing to local extinction. Using a landscape genetics approach, we investigated sloth bear (Melursus ursinus) populations in India's Central Terai landscape-a human-dominated, multi-use region that exemplifies the challenges of conserving wildlife populations in highly fragmented landscapes. Using non-invasively collected fecal samples (n = 209), we identified 66 individuals from 964 genome-wide SNPs generated via ddRAD sequencing. Spatial genetic structuring was not strictly congruent to the protected areas and genetic clusters showed low genetic diversity (mean HE = 0.156 ; mean HO = 0.079) with a heterozygote deficit (mean FIS = 0.323). Further, landscape genetic analyses revealed agriculture as the primary barrier to gene flow across the landscape, followed by proximity to water. Our findings establish the first genetic baseline for sloth bears in this region and suggest that historical population structure and contemporary fragmentation may jointly influence genetic connectivity and diversity across the landscape. We demonstrate the unique utility of non-invasive samples and genome-wide SNP based analyses for poorly studied species of conservation concern, despite experimental and bioinformatic challenges. Our novel insights underscores the importance of such genetic monitoring in fragmented landscapes.

title: Hybridization drives high genetic diversity in the Japanese fire-bellied newt, Cynops pyrrhogaster
authors: Shiroma H, Matsunami M, Shimada T, Matsui M, Nishikawa K, Nagano AJ, Tominaga A.
abstract: Recent advances in evolutionary biology have highlighted the important roles of hybridization and gene flow in shaping genetic structure and diversification in many organisms. The Japanese fire-bellied newt, Cynops pyrrhogaster, comprises multiple diverged mitochondrial DNA lineages. High genetic differentiation and strong reproductive isolation were observed among lineages, suggesting that some of these lineages may represent distinct species. To clarify the population structure and gene flow among lineages, we performed population genetic analyses based on genome-wide double digest restriction site-associated DNA sequencing together with partial mitochondrial cytochrome-b sequences, using samples collected across the species' entire geographic range. Analyses of Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) data revealed three major groups (Northern, Central, and Western groups) with some hybrid populations in the contact zones. Estimation of the evolutionary history using an approximate Bayesian computation approach suggested that the common ancestor of this species first diverged into the Northern and Western groups in the late Miocene and that subsequent hybridization between these two groups gave rise to the Central group in the late Pliocene. An f4-test indicated gene flow from the Western group into the southwestern Central group, as well as that from the Northern group into the northeastern Central group. A mito-nuclear discordant population was also detected within the southwestern Central group, suggesting past hybridization. These results demonstrate that hybridization and subsequent gene flow play a crucial role in the formation of complex population structure and the maintenance of genetic diversity in the Japanese fire-bellied newt.

title: Little sharks in a genomic world: A high-resolution view of population structure in the California horn shark (Heterodontus francisci)
authors: Canfield SJ, Galván-Magaña F, Bowen BW.
abstract: The California horn shark (Heterodontus francisci) is a small demersal elasmobranch distributed along Pacific coastlines from California to Mexico, including several nearshore islands. Previous analyses of mitochondrial control region variation indicated that island populations are genetically distinct from mainland populations, while little to no structure was detected along contiguous coastlines over much larger distances, suggesting that deep-water channels may act as barriers to dispersal. However, this interpretation was inconsistent with the lack of detectable differentiation between the northern Channel Islands (NCIs) and Santa Catalina Island, separated by nearly 100 km of deep, cold water. To reexamine patterns of population connectivity, we used double-digest restriction site-associated DNA sequencing to genotype 3,953 nuclear single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) from 175 specimens sampled across the range of H. francisci. Analyses identified at least five genetically distinct population units and recovered strong differentiation between the NCIs and Santa Catalina Island, supporting the hypothesis that deep-water channels are an important driver of population structure in H. francisci at spatial scales as small as 20 km (FST ≥ 0.020). Shallow but extensive population structure was associated with geographic distance along the mainland Pacific coast, spanning more than 1,200 km of shoreline (FST ≤ 0.013). Overall, our results demonstrate substantial population subdivision across the range of H. francisci and reduced genetic diversity within island populations. These findings highlight the importance of considering population structure in the conservation and management of diminutive demersal sharks and support the development of stock-specific management strategies.

title: Integrating marker-assisted backcross breeding and genomic analysis to obtain thermotolerant tomato genotypes for the fresh market
authors: Graci S, Addonizio M, Giglio D, Francesca S, Barone A.
journal: Molecular breeding : new strategies in plant improvement
abstract:
Current climate change significantly impacts on agriculture, negatively affecting plant growth and development of many agricultural crops including tomato. To adapt to current increase in temperatures, it is essential to develop novel heat tolerant cultivars. The present study describes a backcross breeding program developed to produce new genotypes suitable for the fresh tomato market that exhibit the favorable characteristics of the previously selected thermotolerant genotype E42. This was achieved by converting the determinate plant habitus of E42 to indeterminate. The SP_CAPS marker designed to target a SNP in the self-pruning gene, which is responsible for the plant habitus, enabled us to accelerate the selection of indeterminate plants, thus obtaining nine BC4S1 lines. The evaluation of ten phenotypic traits in two different growth conditions (open field and under plastic tunnel) evidenced the good performances of the BC4S1 lines and the phenotypic recovery of the recurrent parent in all of them. Interestingly, one genotype exceeded the mean yield values of the group when grown in open field. In addition, the analysis of the ddRAD sequencing data revealed a high level of genomic recovery, with only a few variants retained from the donor parents. Clear linkage drag was assessed in almost all the BC4S1 lines around the self-pruning gene that was targeted using Marker Assisted Selection. Altogether, this work provided improved thermotolerant genotypes with high fruit quality that may find place in the tomato fresh market.

Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-026-01730-0.

title: Patterns of genetic variation in a range-expanding fruit fly Zeugodacus tau
authors: Wang YT, Yue L, Cao LJ, Chen JC, Song W, Ma WH, Yang JF, Gao XY, Chen HS, Zhang Y, Tian ZY, Thia JA, Hoffmann AA, Wei SJ, Zhou ZS.
abstract:
Background Range expansion is often accompanied by reduced genetic diversity and increased environmental stress in populations at range edges, potentially constraining adaptive evolution despite strong selection. This study aimed to investigate these processes during the northward range expansion of the fruit fly Zeugodacus tau, an important agricultural pest. We sampled 217 individuals from 11 geographical populations spanning the species' current distribution across China and genotyped them using double-digest restriction-site-associated DNA sequencing (ddRAD-seq).

Results The surveyed populations were genetically differentiated into southwestern and southeastern groups, with an admixed group located in the longitudinal transition zone between them. Northern populations generally exhibited lower genetic diversity than southern populations, whereas populations with admixed ancestry tended to retain higher genetic diversity than non-admixed populations at comparable latitudes. TreeMix supported two historical migration events, and all populations except Shanghai exhibited broadly similar demographic histories. Environmental variables independently explained more genomic variation than geographic variables, both across all populations (53.01% vs 27.28%) and within the admixed group (50.64% vs 17.25%). Genome scans identified candidate SNPs in the admixed group that were potentially associated with responses to environmental stress.

Conclusions Our findings show that the northward range expansion of Z. tau is accompanied by a general decline in genetic diversity, while admixture among differentiated lineages may partially offset this loss. These results highlight the joint roles of demographic history and admixture in shaping genomic variation during range expansion, although the adaptive consequences of admixture remain unresolved. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

title: Contrasting Spatial Genomic Structure in Two Widespread Grassland Species Across Norway Supports Species-Specific Seed Sourcing
authors: Gizaw A, Hanslin HM, Aamlid TS, Borch H, Šípková H, Fossdal CG.
abstract: Ecological restoration typically relies on locally sourced seed material, yet seed sourcing in many countries is based on broad administrative regions rather than empirical genetic data. Whether these generalized zones reflect biologically meaningful population genomic structure, particularly among co-occurring species used together in restoration, remains poorly understood, thus limiting genetically informed restoration practices. Here, we use genome-wide double-digest RAD sequencing (ddRAD-seq) to examine spatial population genomic structure in two widespread perennial grassland species commonly used in restoration in Norway: Silene dioica, an obligately outcrossing species with limited seed dispersal, and Achillea millefolium, a polyploid complex characterized by high gene flow and dispersal capacity. Analysis of 17 populations of S. dioica (355 individuals; 19,200 SNPs) and 23 populations of A. millefolium (428 individuals; 21,294 SNPs) across broad latitudinal and climatic gradients in Norway revealed strikingly contrasting patterns of genetic structure. Silene dioica showed moderate spatial structure, significant isolation-by-distance, and multiple geographically coherent genetic groups, indicating spatially restricted gene flow and supporting the delineation of multiple seed transfer zones. In contrast, A. millefolium showed weak population differentiation, extensive admixture, and little geographic structuring, but significant isolation-by-environment, with annual precipitation emerging as the strongest environmental predictor of genomic differentiation independently of geographic distance, justifying the delineation of three broad genomic zones. Because species-specific life-history traits likely contributed to these patterns, a single generalized seed-sourcing framework can be inadequate even for sympatric species restored together. While the structured genomic patterns in S. dioica support localized seed sourcing, the high connectivity in A. millefolium supports broader transfer zones. Overall, our study highlights the importance of incorporating genomic data into restoration planning by aligning seed transfer distances with species-specific connectivity to reduce genetic risks and maintain evolutionary potential under environmental change.

title: Climate-Associated Genetic Variation in Native and Introduced Populations of Eustenopus villosus, a Biological Control Agent for Yellow Starthistle
authors: Barker BS, Pelosi JA, Sert O, Dlugosch KM.
abstract: Contemporary evolution in biological control systems is rarely studied, though biological agents are repeatedly exposed to novel environmental conditions upon introduction. Their ability to adapt to new conditions could influence management efficacy and reveal important aspects of environmental selection. Using a ddRADseq dataset, we tested for genomic evidence of adaptation to climate in populations of Eustenopus villosus (Boheman, Coleoptera: Curculionidae), the "hairy weevil", which is used in classical biological control for yellow starthistle (Centaurea solstitialis L., Asteraceae) in the western United States. We first estimated population structure in E. villosus across our samples of the native and introduced ranges and then used six complementary genotype-environment association analyses to identify single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with climate in both native and introduced populations. Additionally, we used historical release records to categorize sampling sites according to their serial founding history and test for impacts of this history on total and putatively adaptive genomic variation in the introductions. We also tested whether candidate loci associated with climate in the native range exhibit similar associations in the introductions, or if new associations have evolved. We identified many candidate loci in both native and introduced populations and found little evidence of a decline in genomic variation, which suggests that serial founding events did not prevent climatic adaptation. Candidate loci differed between native and introduced populations, indicating that local adaptation has occurred in different regions of the genome after introduction of E. villosus. Our findings suggest an important role for novel contemporary adaptation in this biological control system and provide insight into how genetic variation can persist in biological control agents through introduction and serial founding events.

title: Genome-wide SNP analysis of genetic diversity and selection signatures in ​Black ​Bengal goats
authors: Nayak SS, Devadharshini K, Ranjith G, Rath PK, Verma SK, Rajawat D, Panigrahi M.
journal: Mammalian genome : official journal of the International Mammalian Genome Society
abstract: The Black Bengal goat, a well-known breed of the Indian subcontinent, is valued for its excellent meat quality, high reproductive efficiency, and ability to thrive under diverse agroclimatic conditions. In this study, genetic diversity and selection signatures were investigated using SNP genotyping data from 90 animals using the ddRAD sequencing approach. Genetic diversity parameters, effective population size (Ne), and selection signatures were evaluated using Tajima's D, composite likelihood ratio (CLR), integrated haplotype score (iHS), and runs of homozygosity (ROH) analyses. Historical analysis of Ne revealed a peak value of 4,930, approximately 368 generations ago, followed by a steady decline to 366 around 13 generations ago. The observed heterozygosity (0.229 ± 0.149) was lower than the expected heterozygosity (0.275 ± 0.139), indicating a deficiency of heterozygotes in the population. The current Ne estimate of 158.4 suggests a reduction in population size over time. Using multiple complementary approaches, we identified 138 genomic regions under positive selection, encompassing 743 genes. Gene Ontology analysis highlighted significant enrichment of negative regulation of complement activation (LOC102169502, LOC102169786), positive regulation of interleukin-12 production (IL12B, IRF8, LEP, MDK), and type II interferon production (IRF8, IL12B, TYK2, CD14), indicating immune regulation and host defense. The candidate genes and enriched pathways identified in this study were mainly associated with immune function, fear response, adaptation, learning, cognition, and visual perception. These findings provide insights into the resilience and adaptation of the Black Bengal goats and may support future breeding and conservation efforts of the indigenous breed.

title: Genetic Diversity and Putative Origin of the Bait Polychaete, Diopatra aciculata Knox and Cameron  (Annelida: Onuphidae), Occurring in South Africa
authors: Schoeman S, Matthee CA, Hull K, Simon CA.
abstract: The bait polychaete Diopatra aciculata is commercially farmed in Australia and is collected as bait in several South African estuaries. Despite its widespread use, the species' geographic origin remains uncertain, hindering management efforts within sensitive estuarine ecosystems. Mitochondrial Cytochrome Oxidase subunit I (mtCOI) data and ddRAD-generated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were used to gain insight into the origin and genetic diversity of D. aciculata. A total of 204 individuals were collected from an aquaculture farm in Australia and the Knysna, Keurbooms, and Swartkops Estuaries in South Africa. The mtCOI analyses supported the monophyly of D. aciculata and revealed lower genetic diversity in the South African population compared to the Australian population. Both marker sets revealed significant genetic differentiation between the continental populations that are naturally isolated by the Indian Ocean basin. The SNP dataset revealed low intrapopulation genetic diversity for both the Australian and South African populations. The discordant genetic diversity findings between the mtCOI and SNP datasets may be attributed to the differences in the evolutionary rate of the two marker systems. In addition, the low genomic diversity observed in the SNP dataset is consistent with the effects of captive breeding in the Australian aquaculture population; consequently, the effect of sampling bias cannot be excluded. However, the mtCOI signal of reduced diversity in South Africa is consistent with an introduced population and both mtCOI and SNP-based RASP analyses recovered Australian samples in a basal position, suggesting Australia as the plausible origin. This highlights the need for precautionary conservation efforts to prevent further spread.
